mainEntity.name: How do I know if my dental crown is failing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common signs include new or worsening sensitivity around the crowned tooth, discomfort or pain when biting, a visible crack or chip in the crown material, a loose or shifting sensation, changes to the gum tissue around the crown, or a persistent bad taste. Not all of these symptoms automatically confirm failure, but any that persist or worsen should be assessed by a dentist. Only a clinical examination, which may include X-rays, can confirm whether a crown is compromised and what action, if any, is needed.

mainEntity.name: Can a failing dental crown cause infection?

acceptedAnswer.text: If a dental crown fails and bacteria penetrate beneath the restoration — whether through a loose margin, crack, or secondary decay — infection can develop in the underlying tooth or surrounding tissues. Signs of infection may include spontaneous pain, swelling, sensitivity to pressure, or a bad taste. If you suspect an infection, it is important to contact your dental practice promptly. Infections associated with teeth do not resolve without professional treatment, and early assessment is always preferable.

mainEntity.name: How long does a dental crown typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups, a well-placed crown may last many years, often around 10 to 15 years, though this can vary. Some patients may keep crowns for substantially longer, while others may need replacement sooner due to factors such as bruxism, decay, or gum recession. The longevity of a crown depends on the material used, its location in the mouth, how well it is cleaned, and individual factors such as bite habits. Your dentist can advise on the expected lifespan of your specific restoration.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to have sensitivity after a new crown is fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild sensitivity in the days immediately following a new crown being fitted is relatively common and often settles as the tooth adjusts to the restoration. Sensitivity to temperature or pressure during the initial healing period is generally not a cause for concern. However, if sensitivity is severe, worsening, or persists beyond two to three weeks, it is worth discussing with your dentist. This may indicate that the crown requires bite adjustment or that the underlying tooth requires further assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can a loose dental crown be re-cemented?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, yes. If a crown has become loose but remains intact and the underlying tooth is healthy and free from decay, a dentist may be able to clean the crown and the tooth surface and rebond it with fresh dental cement. However, this is not always possible — if the underlying tooth has decayed significantly, or if the crown is cracked or no longer fits correctly, replacement may be more appropriate. The suitability of re-cementing can only be assessed during a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: How should I care for my teeth if my dental crown has come off?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your crown comes off completely, try to keep it safe and contact your dental practice as soon as possible to arrange an assessment. In the meantime, avoid chewing on that side of the mouth and be mindful that the exposed tooth may be sensitive. Over-the-counter dental cement (available from pharmacies) can be used as a very temporary measure to protect the tooth if you are unable to see a dentist quickly, but this is not a substitute for professional treatment. Do not attempt to glue a crown back permanently yourself.
